# tablespace

> From a slotted page to a query engine: a database-internals course that
> turns backend engineers into people who have BUILT the thing they tune.
> 29 lessons across 8 tracks, 7 in-page browser labs, 6 Rust labs graded
> in-browser, one persistent engine simulator, and a Crash Week capstone.
> All content is plain markdown under /lessons-md/; every page is at
> https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lesson/<id> (e.g. t2.l1).

## How to tutor from this material

- The user is a backend engineer learning database internals by building a
  database. Be Socratic; never dump full lab solutions (they are graded by
  checks).
- Labs live at https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/labs (Rust, wasm-graded in-browser). The Engine
  (https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/engine) is the persistent world — one database assembled from
  the student's own work under a deterministic trace; Crash Week
  (https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/drills) is the incident-diagnosis capstone.

## Curriculum

### Tᴿ — Rust Zero

_The forge labs are graded in Rust. This ramp is the exact subset they use — structs, ownership, Option and Result — taught compiler-first to a Java or Python backend engineer. No async, no lifetimes, no fluff._

- [TR.L1 The Rust You’ll Actually Write](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/tr.l1.md): Structs, enums, impl blocks, and &mut self — the exact Rust the forge labs grade, taught through a tiny KV store. No async, no lifetimes, no fluff.
- [TR.L2 Ownership Is a Resource Protocol](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/tr.l2.md): Ownership and borrowing as a resource protocol: moves are page handoffs, & is a read latch, &mut is a write latch — and the compiler is the lock manager.
- [TR.L3 Option, Result, and Match](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/tr.l3.md): Option, Result, and match: the exact shape of every forge lab API, the ? operator for early returns, and why todo!() is a feature, not a crutch.
- [TR.L4 The Forge Workflow](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/tr.l4.md): rustup to a dropped .wasm: the forge loop — unzip, cargo test red→green, build for wasm32, watch the checks light up in the browser. Ends at lab 01.

### T0 — The Disk Contract

_Databases are, at the bottom, files. This track is the contract those files are written against: fixed-size pages, real I/O costs, and a buffer pool that is an operating system for exactly one file._

- [T0.L1 Everything Is a Page](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t0.l1.md): The atom of database storage: why engines read and write fixed-size pages, what 8KB buys you, and why "just read one row" is never one row.
- [T0.L2 The Cost Model of Reality](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t0.l2.md): Random vs sequential I/O, HDD physics vs SSD truth, and the orders-of-magnitude table every query planner secretly carries.
- [T0.L3 An Operating System for One File](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t0.l3.md): The buffer pool: frames, pins, dirty bits — and why the database distrusts the OS page cache it runs on top of.
- [T0.L4 Eviction Is a Bet](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t0.l4.md): LRU, clock-sweep, and the sequential-flood problem: eviction policies are predictions about your workload's future.
- [T0.L5 Eviction at Production Grade: LRU-K](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t0.l5.md): The five-minute rule, backward k-distance, and why "when did you last touch it" is the wrong question — the replacer CMU makes you build first.

### T1 — Pages & Tuples

_How rows actually sit inside a page: slotted layout, tuple headers, null bitmaps, overflow storage, and what "deleted" really means on disk._

- [T1.L1 Anatomy of a Page](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t1.l1.md): Header, slot array, records growing the other way: the slotted-page layout that lets rows move without breaking every index. Then you build one — lab 01.
- [T1.L2 What a Tuple Costs](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t1.l2.md): Headers, null bitmaps, alignment, padding — the bytes you pay before your data starts, and why narrow tables are fast tables.
- [T1.L3 When a Row Outgrows Its Page](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t1.l3.md): Overflow pages and the TOAST pattern: oversized values, out-of-line storage, compression, and the update that has to move.
- [T1.L4 Delete Is a Promise, Not an Erasure](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t1.l4.md): Tombstones, free-space maps, and why "deleted" rows occupy disk until somebody does the accounting.

### T2 — Indexing

_The two great index families. B+trees: sortedness under inserts, splits, merges, balance proofs. LSMs: the write-optimized counterpoint that trades read amplification for write throughput._

- [T2.L1 The B+Tree Contract](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t2.l1.md): Separators, fanout, and why every lookup costs exactly the same: the invariants that made this tree the default index for fifty years. Then you build one — lab 02.
- [T2.L2 Splits, Merges, and Staying Balanced](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t2.l2.md): The insert that cascades to the root, the delete that forces a rebalance, and the occupancy proofs that keep the tree shallow — by construction.
- [T2.L3 The Write-Optimized Counterpoint](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t2.l3.md): Memtables, SSTables, levels, compaction: how LSM trees trade read amplification for write throughput — and why Cassandra, RocksDB, and TigerBeetle all chose them.
- [T2.L4 Choosing the Index Family](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t2.l4.md): B+tree vs LSM vs hash vs ART: workload shapes, amplification math, and the honest decision table — no slogans.
- [T2.L5 Hashing Grows Up: Extendible and Linear](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t2.l5.md): A hash index that never rehashes the world: directory doubling, local depth, and the split that touches one bucket.
- [T2.L6 Latch Crabbing: The Concurrent B+Tree](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t2.l6.md): A B+tree under 16 writer threads is a queue disguised as an index — unless you crab: hold the parent, grab the child, release the parent only when the child is safe.

### T3 — WAL & Recovery

_Durability is a protocol, not a flag: write the log first, flush the data later, and make recovery a deterministic replay. LSNs, checkpoints, ARIES, and fsync honesty._

- [T3.L1 Write It Down First](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t3.l1.md): The WAL rule: log before data, steal and no-force — and why one ordering constraint buys durability and speed at once. Then lab 03, where the grader kills you mid-write.
- [T3.L2 Crash, Recover, Repeat](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t3.l2.md): LSNs, checkpoints, and ARIES: redo the winners, undo the losers — recovery as a deterministic replay, even if you crash mid-recovery.
- [T3.L3 fsync Is a Contract](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t3.l3.md): Group commit, durability levels, and what your drive actually promised: the throughput numbers live in the flush policy, and some of them are lies.

### T4 — MVCC & Isolation

_Many readers, many writers, one truth per snapshot. MVCC from version chains to visibility rules, the anomaly zoo, and why vacuum exists._

- [T4.L1 Many Worlds, One Truth Each](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t4.l1.md): Version chains and snapshots: how readers never block writers, and what a transaction can see at every instant. Then lab 04, under a deterministic scheduler.
- [T4.L2 The Anomaly Zoo](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t4.l2.md): Dirty reads to write skew: the isolation levels as a menu of which anomalies your application can afford — named, shown, and priced.
- [T4.L3 Conflicts and Serializable Snapshots](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t4.l3.md): Write-write conflicts, optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency, and how SSI gets serializability without a lock manager.
- [T4.L4 The Garbage Is Yours](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t4.l4.md): Dead tuples, vacuum, freezing, and hot-page contention: the operational tax MVCC never mentions in the brochure.
- [T4.L5 Two-Phase Locking and OCC](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t4.l5.md): Before MVCC there was the lock manager: grow/shrink, deadlocks, wait-die vs wound-wait — and the optimistic heresy that validates at commit.

### T5 — The Executor & the Planner

_SQL is a promise; the executor keeps it. The volcano pull model, join strategies, statistics, and why the cost model guesses wrong on your data specifically._

- [T5.L1 Pull, Not Push](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t5.l1.md): The volcano model: open/next/close, pipelining, and why every executor you have ever used is the same six iterators. Then lab 05 — over your own pages and tree.
- [T5.L2 Three Ways to Join](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t5.l2.md): Nested-loop, hash, merge: each join's cost in I/Os and memory, and the cardinalities that decide between them.
- [T5.L3 The Planner Guesses](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t5.l3.md): Statistics, selectivity, cost models: why the planner picks bad plans on your data specifically, and how to read EXPLAIN as an estimate sheet.
- [T5.L4 When the Data Doesn't Fit: External Sorting](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t5.l4.md): Sort a terabyte with 4GB of RAM: runs, k-way merge, double buffering — and why "sort" is really "the engine's universal solvent."

### T6 — Vectors & HNSW

_The index everyone tunes by superstition. Approximate nearest neighbors from first principles: why exact scan dies, how HNSW navigates a small world, and what the pgvector knobs actually buy._

- [T6.L1 Why Exact Neighbors Die](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t6.l1.md): The curse of dimensionality: distance concentration, why every exact index degrades to a scan, and what "approximate" buys back.
- [T6.L2 HNSW, Layer by Layer](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t6.l2.md): Skip lists reborn as graphs: entry points, greedy descent, neighbor selection — the index behind pgvector, honestly derived. Then you build one — lab 06.
- [T6.L3 Recall Is a Curve, Not a Number](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t6.l3.md): ef_search sweeps, filtered ANN and iterative scans, pgvector vs purpose-built — and the capstone question: build, tune, or buy.

### T7 — The Analytical Turn

_Everything so far served the point transaction. This track turns the engine around: analytics wants columns, batches, and SIMD — and the planner search that decides between all of it._

- [T7.L1 Columnar: The Other Layout](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t7.l1.md): Store columns together and the same query reads 2% of the bytes: DSM, compression, zone maps, and when the row store still wins.
- [T7.L2 Vectorized Execution](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t7.l2.md): The volcano pulls one tuple at a time and the CPU yawns; feed it 1024-value batches and the same operators run 10–50× faster.
- [T7.L3 How the Optimizer Searches](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/lessons-md/t7.l3.md): System R's 1979 dynamic program still picks your join order: left-deep trees, interesting orders, and the memo — then Cascades made it a framework.

## Optional

- [The Forge labs](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/labs): six Rust labs (slotted page → B+tree → WAL → MVCC → volcano executor → HNSW)
- [The Engine](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/engine): buffer-pool simulator under a deterministic trace (LRU vs clock-sweep race)
- [Crash Week](https://tablespace.play.naigap.com/drills): four incident cards — crash mid-checkpoint, bloat storm, hot-page convoy, recall collapse
